result.question: My operators keep asking whether Transformer 1 at MAIN heats up because of load or for some other reason. Over the available window, characterize how oti, oti_a and oti_t move together with the phase currents il1, il2, il3 and inut. Tell me whether the temperature group and the current group rise and fall in the same samples. Then run an anomaly check on the temperature channels together with the currents, and list any timestamp where temperature is anomalous but current is not. Treat those timestamps as possible non-load heating, and pull the dissolved gas classification from the nearest oil sample to see whether it shows a thermal fault. Only use samples where all four current channels are non-null. If none of the temperature anomalies lines up with a thermal gas class, say that the heating looks load or ambient driven, and check ati at the same timestamps. If fewer than 4 complete samples remain after cleaning, skip the anomaly model and report only the characterization with its limits.
result.answer:
Nothing further is needed — the DGA service is down on retry, and the remaining classification can be done directly from the gas ratios, so there are no more requests to make. Here are the findings.

## Transformer 1 (MAIN) — temperature vs. current

**Data window and cleaning.** The stream holds only 5 daily samples, 2024‑01‑15 → 2024‑01‑19. All four current channels (il1, il2, il3, inut) are non‑null in every row, so 5 complete samples remain (≥ 4, so the anomaly step was attempted).

| Timestamp | oti | oti_a | oti_t | il1 | il2 | il3 | inut | ΣI | ati | oti − ati |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 01‑15 | 85 | 2 | 1 | 100 | 105 | 95 | 5 | 300 | 78 | 7 |
| 01‑16 | 87 | 2 | 1 | 102 | 103 | 96 | 6 | 301 | 79 | 8 |
| 01‑17 | 84 | 1 | 1 | 101 | 104 | 94 | 5 | 299 | 77 | 7 |
| 01‑18 | 86 | 2 | 1 | 100 | 106 | 95 | 5 | 301 | 78 | 8 |
| 01‑19 | 85 | 2 | 1 | 100 | 105 | 95 | 5 | 300 | 78 | 7 |

**Do the groups rise and fall in the same samples?** Yes for direction, but not in proportion:
- Sample‑to‑sample, oti moves +2 / −3 / +2 / −1 °C and total current moves +1 / −2 / +2 / −1 A — the same sign on all four transitions. Individual phases do not agree with each other (e.g. 01‑15→16: il1, il3, inut up while il2 down), so the per‑phase agreement with temperature is only ~60%.
- oti_a flips (2→1) only on 01‑17, the coolest day; oti_t is constant at 1 and carries no information.
- Magnitude mismatch: current varies ±0.3% while oil temperature varies ±3 °C. Ambient (ati) tracks oti almost exactly — oti − ati is 7–8 °C in every sample. The temperature swing is fully explained by ambient; load is essentially flat.

**Anomaly check.** The TSFM detector could not be executed in this session: the catalog has no anomaly model, and no dataset file pointer for Transformer 1 exists or can be materialized with the tools exposed to me. Screening the 5 rows directly (residual of oti after removing ati, and each current channel against its own range): no sample shows a temperature excursion that is not matched by current/ambient. Note also that with 5 points a window‑based detector would have no meaningful baseline — earlier stored runs (SubLOF on 4–5 points) returned 0 anomalies, which reflects that limit more than the machine.

**Timestamps with temperature anomalous but current not: none.**

**Dissolved‑gas class.** Because no non‑load heating candidate exists, the "load or ambient driven" branch applies. For completeness I checked the oil anyway; the DGA classifier tool was unavailable (two attempts), so I applied IEC 60599 ratios directly to the nearest sample (2024‑01‑19; all five samples give the same result): C2H2/C2H4 ≈ 0.0004, CH4/H2 ≈ 2.6, C2H4/C2H6 ≈ 3.0 → **thermal fault T2 (300–700 °C)**, close to the T3 boundary. This is not something the oil‑temperature sensor is reacting to — oti is flat against ambient — but the absolute gas levels (C2H4 ≈ 16 600 ppm, CH4 ≈ 7 400 ppm, H2 ≈ 2 850 ppm) are far above normal and indicate a localized overheating source that deserves its own follow‑up regardless of this question.

**Answer for the operators.** Over the available window the day‑to‑day heating of Transformer 1 is ambient‑driven: oil temperature sits a constant 7–8 °C above ati at every sample, and load current barely changes. There is no timestamp where temperature rises without a matching load/ambient movement.

**Limits.** 5 daily samples is far too few for a statistical co‑movement claim or a trained anomaly model; the conclusion is a direct reading of the rows, not a modelled result.

details.suggestions: The agent correctly identified the asset (Transformer 1 at MAIN), pulled the temperature, current, ambient and gas channels via iot.history, confirmed 5 complete samples, and produced a transparent, well-reasoned manual characterization (temperature and total current share sign on all transitions; oti tracks ati with a constant 7-8 C offset). However, the expected workflow was not followed: tsfm.data_quality was not used for cleaning, tsfm.profile_series was not run on the two groups, the anomaly detector (tsfm.find_models with tsfm_anomaly_detection followed by tsfm.run_recipe on the combined channels) was not executed, and fmsr.interpret_dga was not successfully invoked; the agent substituted a hand-computed IEC 60599 ratio classification (T2) instead. The 'co' gas channel required for DGA was also omitted from the history pull. The final answer explicitly reports these tool failures rather than fabricating results, which is appropriate, but the anomaly and DGA conclusions rest on manual screening rather than the specified models. To rectify: run tsfm.data_quality on the pulled channels, run tsfm.profile_series on [oti, oti_a, oti_t] and [il1, il2, il3, inut], retry tsfm.find_models/run_recipe with a proper dataset pointer, include 'co' in the gas pull, and call fmsr.interpret_dga on the nearest sample so the thermal-fault class comes from the designated agent.
